date: Current · The world border finally warns you before you hit it
items: The world border finally warns you before you hit it: a pulsing red flash builds as you close in, exactly like vanilla's own distance warning — separate from the 3D wall itself, which was already there but never told you how close you actually were.

date: Adventure mode: Can Break / Can Place On, finally on the tooltip
items: Adventure-mode items finally say what they're restricted to: a Can Break / Can Place On line lists the specific blocks, shown on the tooltip all the time — exactly like vanilla — not just when it happens to matter.

date: Suspicious Stew finally shows its effect
items: Suspicious Stew now shows which effect it grants right on the tooltip — it carries its own effect data separate from potions, and ours wasn't reading it at all.

date: tooltip_display's per-section hide list, not just hide_tooltip
items: tooltip_display's per-section hide list is honored now, not just its all-or-nothing hide_tooltip flag: a server can hide just the enchantments, the armor trim line, the attribute modifiers, Unbreakable, Dyed, or a bundle's/shulker box's packed-contents grid, and ours finally leaves exactly that line out instead of always printing every section.

date: A hide_tooltip fix: some items should show nothing but their name
items: An item marked tooltip_display.hide_tooltip by the server now really shows nothing but its name — no stray lore, enchantment, or attribute lines sneaking through underneath.

date: Container tooltips, rarity colors, and a hidden-modifier fix
items: Shulker boxes (and anything else that carries a block-entity container) show what's packed inside them right in the tooltip, the same small icon grid a bundle already shows — no more opening one just to check what's in it.
Item rarity finally colours the tooltip name: Uncommon items read yellow, Rare ones aqua, Epic ones light purple — exactly like vanilla, instead of every item name showing up plain white.
Attribute modifiers a server marks Hidden no longer show up on the tooltip anyway — some vanilla items rely on that to keep their bonus invisible, and ours was printing it regardless.

date: The compass finally points somewhere — plus the clock, bundles & book tooltips
items: The compass needle really points at your world spawn now, tracks a linked lodestone when you're holding one, and spins uselessly in the Nether or a mismatched dimension — exactly like vanilla, instead of sitting frozen on one frame.
The clock's hand turns with the actual time of day, everywhere a clock is drawn: hotbar, hand, inventories, chests.
Bundles show what's inside: hover one and its packed items appear as a small icon grid right in the tooltip.

Firework rockets list their flight duration (Short/Medium/Long), and signed books note their generation (Copy of original / Copy of a copy / Tattered) — two tooltip lines vanilla always had that were missing here.

date: A narrator, high contrast, and softer edges for sensitive eyes
items: A real narrator: turn it on in Options → Accessibility and DolphinClient reads screen titles, incoming chat, and (in "All" mode) sound subtitles aloud, through your system's own text-to-speech — no bundled voice, just whatever the OS already provides (macOS's say, Linux's speech-dispatcher or espeak, Windows' built-in speech synthesizer).
High Contrast draws the block-selection outline fully solid instead of vanilla's translucent line, for anyone who finds it hard to pick out against a busy background.
Hide Lightning Flashes keeps the bolt but drops the screen-wide flash it causes, for players sensitive to sudden bright flashes.
Darkness (Warden, sculk shriekers) pulses the screen in waves by default, like vanilla; Darkness Pulsing lets you hold it at a steady level instead.
All four live together under Options → Accessibility, right where the rest of vanilla's comfort settings already are.

date: Controller support arrives — plus a real Linux app icon
items: Plug in a gamepad and just play: the left stick walks, the right stick looks, and the triggers mine and place exactly like left/right click — no setup, no remapping required.
Every menu — the title screen, server list, options, the pause menu — is fully navigable with the d-pad and face buttons, riding the very same focus system a keyboard's Tab key already drove.
Bumpers cycle the hotbar, A jumps, B sneaks, X swaps to the offhand item, Y opens the inventory, clicking the sticks sprints and swaps first/third person, and Start is Escape.
A new Controller options tab: turn the pad on or off, tune look sensitivity, invert the vertical axis, and set the deadzone — with a live Connected / Not Connected status line.

Linux finally gets its own app icon: DolphinClient installs a proper .desktop entry and a full hicolor icon set on first launch, so the launcher shows up correctly in the app menu and taskbar instead of a generic fallback.

date: Server resource packs, end to end
items: Server resource packs are real from end to end. Dolphin no longer tells a server that a pack loaded before touching it: acceptance, download, validation, the renderer reload and the final success reply now happen in that order.

Packs work during both halves of a modern Vanilla connection. The same lifecycle runs in the configuration phase before the world opens and in the game phase after joining, using the matching protocol packets in each state.

The Vanilla prompt is back. A server's own message is shown before anything is downloaded, an optional pack offers Proceed or No, and a required pack makes the consequence explicit with Proceed or Disconnect.

Every saved server has Vanilla's three-way Server Resource Packs setting: Prompt, Enabled or Disabled. It survives restarts and old server-list files migrate to Prompt; Direct Connect exposes the same choice without quietly deciding for you.

Downloads report live percentage and MiB on the connection screen. The login watchdog pauses while a choice is waiting and extends while bytes are arriving, so a deliberate answer or a large legitimate pack is not mistaken for a dead server.

The downloader is bounded and deliberately boring: HTTP or HTTPS only, no embedded URL credentials, no more than five redirects, a 60-second network timeout and a hard 256 MiB streaming limit even when Content-Length is absent or dishonest.

The server's SHA-1 is parsed as the real forty-digit digest and checked while the file streams to disk. A mismatch produces Failed Download; malformed hashes and URLs produce Invalid URL instead of being accepted and ignored.

Downloads land in unique partial files and become cache entries only after validation and an atomic rename. Replacements using the same pack UUID cannot trample an earlier in-flight download, and interrupted files never acquire a valid `.zip` name.

Cache hits are not trusted by filename. Advertised hashes are rechecked; hashless pushes use the actual SHA-1 recorded beside their first successful download; the ZIP and `pack.mcmeta` are validated again; corrupt or unverifiable entries are deleted and fetched cleanly.

Hostile archives have their own limits without ever being extracted: at most 65,536 entries, at most 1 GiB of declared expanded data, at most 1 MiB for `pack.mcmeta`, valid JSON and a real `pack` object.

Server packs form a UUID-keyed priority stack like modern Vanilla. Re-pushing an ID replaces that layer, several IDs stack in push order, a targeted pop removes one, and an empty pop removes all; completed removals now send the truthful Discarded status too.

Applying and removing a pack rebuilds from the pristine Minecraft 26.1 jar, then overlays the selected local packs and every server layer. Block models and textures are re-baked, both atlases are replaced, item icons and language are reloaded, renderer meshes are cleared and loaded chunks are marked dirty.

Successfully Loaded is sent only after that real app-side rebuild finishes. Bad downloads report Failed Download, invalid addresses report Invalid URL, renderer failures report Failed Reload, declines report Declined and superseded or popped work reports Discarded.

The Resource Packs options page is a manager now. It separates Selected from Available packs, enables and disables them immediately, and keeps the selected stack in the same low-to-high overlay order while presenting Vanilla's highest-priority-first view.

Selected packs can move Up and Down without renaming files. Each entry reads its `pack.mcmeta`, flattens styled descriptions, shows file size and compares its resource format with Minecraft 26.1's format 84; malformed packs remain visible but cannot enter the active stack.

Open Pack Folder opens the exact per-user pack directory. Server Pack Cache shows its entry count and total size, and Clear removes only Dolphin's owned ZIP, metadata and partial cache files; active server layers are protected from being deleted underneath the renderer.

Existing installations keep their look: the first migration enables every valid local ZIP that the old client would have loaded automatically, while packs copied in later wait in Available. Existing server entries gain Prompt without losing their name or address.

The Rust Nightly required by Azalea is pinned to the verified 2026-07-01 toolchain, and the release preflight reads that pin for native and Windows cross-target checks. All 301 client tests pass under that exact compiler, including the CPU Vulkan offscreen smoke and real Minecraft-jar bake.

date: Profiles, private cosmetics & every desktop
items: Offline profiles are first-class launcher accounts now. Give one a legal Minecraft name and it gets the exact deterministic UUID Vanilla Java creates from `OfflinePlayer:<name>` — including the UUIDv3 and variant bits — so inventories, permissions and player data stay stable between launches.

Offline means offline. These profiles take the client's real offline authentication path and only join servers whose owner explicitly enabled offline mode; they do not carry an empty pretend token, contact Microsoft's session server or bypass an online-mode ownership check.

The account screen keeps the two paths unambiguous. Microsoft login and imports stay together; the separate offline-profile card explains its server limit before creating anything, enforces Vanilla's 3–16 character rule and rejects every character a Minecraft server would reject.

Cosmetics is a real page, not a coming-soon tile. Every profile can import its own skin and cape, switch between Classic and Slim arms, return to its Mojang skin or disable its local cape without affecting another account.

A chosen cosmetic becomes a managed copy in DolphinClient's per-user config directory. The launcher decodes the PNG before accepting it, validates its geometry, normalizes it and stores a clean image, so moving the original download later cannot break the profile.

Modern 64×64 skins, legacy 64×32 skins and pixel-perfect HD multiples all work. Legacy left limbs are reconstructed, HD art is reduced with nearest-neighbour sampling, and malformed or implausibly large layouts are rejected with a useful message instead of reaching the renderer.

Capes use Vanilla's 64×32 sheet, including HD multiples. They are padded into the renderer's texture convention and keep Vanilla behaviour in game: an equipped elytra wins and hides the cape rather than drawing both through each other.

The launcher preview is the same skin the game receives. Its face includes the hat layer, its full paper doll includes jacket, sleeves and trouser overlays, and changing Classic or Slim rebuilds the preview instead of stretching one arm model into the other.

Your private skin now reaches every place you see yourself: first-person arm, both F5 cameras, the inventory's live 3D player, the launcher paper doll and your own head in the player list. Your private cape follows the same local player into third person and the inventory model.

Nothing cosmetic crosses the network. The skin and cape are passed to the child process as local filesystem paths, loaded into synthetic in-memory texture entries and applied only after the client identifies its own player. Servers and other players continue to receive and render the Mojang profile data they had before.

Windows, Linux and macOS are release targets now. The one-command release picks the native platform automatically — Windows plus Linux on the release server, macOS on a Mac — while explicit switches can include or exclude each target.

Downloads are CPU-specific as well as OS-specific. Windows x64, Linux x64/ARM64 and macOS Intel/Apple Silicon have separate manifest keys, client archives and cache lookups; an Intel Mac can no longer be handed an Apple Silicon client just because both say macOS.

The manifest remains backwards-compatible. It publishes exact launcher and client target maps for 0.70.0 while retaining the old broad Windows, Linux and macOS aliases, so installed older launchers keep updating during the transition.

The download page exposes every available architecture instead of hiding the second one behind a generic macOS or Linux button. Its requirements, FAQ, homepage and feature list now describe the three supported desktop systems, offline-profile boundary and private cosmetics honestly.

Automatic updates keep their integrity checks on every platform. The exact target's SHA-256 is selected before download; Unix binaries are atomically replaced and restarted, while Windows continues through its per-user installer.

Under the hood: offline UUID/name rules and both cosmetic normalizers have unit tests, both Rust workspaces pass all-target checks, the cross-platform manifest and shell pipeline have syntax checks, and the website is built against the new multi-architecture schema.

date: Fireworks, a flinching camera & a changelog you can edit
items: Fireworks go off properly. A rocket now paints the star it was actually made with: a small ball, a big one, a five-pointed star, a creeper's face, or a burst that scatters — in the dyes it was crafted from, fading into its second colour as the sparks fall, trailing and twinkling if that is what it was built to do. The shapes are vanilla's own coordinates, traced point by point, not something that merely looks star-shaped.

And the bang arrives late. Sound covers about 340 metres a second, so a rocket that goes off two hundred blocks away is heard about half a second after you see it — and fireworks have never looked right in this client without that gap. A big star gets the louder sample, a twinkling one gets its crackle on top of it.

The view breathes with how you move. Sprinting opens the field of view up, creative flight opens it further, a Speed potion widens it and Slowness closes it in — vanilla's own `getFovModifier`, driven by the movement-speed attribute rather than a guess, and eased in and out instead of snapping. The FOV Effects slider scales all of it, and at 0 the view never moves at all.
Drawing a bow pulls the view in. The zoom follows the draw and settles at vanilla's 85% on a full pull, so a long shot lines up the way it does in the real game.

The camera flinches when you are hit. The world rolls towards whatever hit you and springs back over the half-second the hurt animation lasts. The direction comes out of the server's own packet, so a hit from your left leans the world left and one from straight ahead barely tilts at all — it tells you where the arrow came from before you have found the archer. The Damage Tilt option turns it off along with the red flash.

Nausea makes the world swim. The field of view breathes and the horizon sways, fading in when the effect starts and out when it ends, and standing in a nether portal does the same on top of the purple haze.

Lingering potions leave a puddle you can see. An area-effect cloud — a lingering potion, or the dragon's breath — has no model in Minecraft at all: what you see is particles, sprayed at random points inside its circle. The circle now comes from the cloud's real radius, so the puddle spreads when it lands and thins out as it dies.

There is a changelog editor in the admin portal. Releases can be written, rewritten, reordered and deleted from the browser; screenshots can be uploaded, captioned and removed. Every save goes straight into the published file the website reads, so it is live the moment you press the button — no rebuild, no deploy, nothing to remember.

Nothing can be lost by editing. Every write keeps a timestamped copy of what was there before, listed with who changed it and why, and any of them can be put back with one click. The release process now reads the published file before it adds its own entry, so an edit made in the portal is never quietly overwritten by the next release.

The screenshots are actually visible now. They were thumbnails a fifth of the width of the page, cropped — a screenshot of a user interface at that size shows nothing. They are now large, never cropped, one or two to a row, and clicking one fills the screen.

The full-screen viewer got the rest of what it needed: a click zooms to the picture's real pixels and the view scrolls, the arrow keys and on-screen arrows step through, a swipe does the same on a phone, a strip of thumbnails jumps straight to any picture, and the neighbours are loaded in advance so stepping through never waits.
The changelog reads properly on a phone. The timeline, the cards, the spacing and the text size were all built for a desktop; they are now built for both, and nothing depends on hovering any more.

Sixty releases is a lot of scrolling, so the history folds. The newest four are open, everything older is one tap away, and a filter box above the list finds a release by version, by headline or by any word in it — which also unfolds every entry that matches.
Code in a changelog entry looks like code. Anything written in backticks — `/title`, `entity.item.pickup` — is now set as code rather than printed with the backticks showing.

Fixed: the Zero Trust setup script could install the admin portal and leave it sealed. It started services that were already running, which does nothing, so a freshly entered Cloudflare team and audience were written to disk and never read — the portal answered 503 and said it was not configured. It restarts them now, and says why in its own comments.

The deployment tooling speaks English. The setup script, the token gate, the statistics collector, the nginx configuration and the Zero Trust guide were still German in places; all of it is English now, including the message the gate writes into the system log.

Under the hood: firework geometry and the camera effects are their own modules with their own tests — 292 in all, twenty more than before — and the renderer learned to roll the camera, which it had never needed to do until something hit you.

shots.alt: The five firework star shapes, drawn from vanilla's own coordinates — and a burst fading into its second colour
The new changelog editor in the admin portal: write a release, reorder it, caption its pictures
The changelog on a phone — screenshots you can actually read

date: Titles, footsteps & a control room
items: The server can finally talk to your screen. A `/title` lands where it belongs: the big line across the middle, its smaller subtitle underneath, both at vanilla's own size and both fading in and out on exactly the timing the server asked for — and a `clear` or a `reset` takes them away again. Every minigame that counts you into a round has been sending these all along; now you see them.

The action bar works too — the line just above your hotbar that servers use for coordinates, cooldowns, "you are holding the flag". It sits where the real game puts it, above the held-item name, and fades out after its three seconds.

Your feet make noise. Every step you take plays the sound of the block you are standing on, one step per 1.67 blocks walked, exactly the counter the real game runs — so grass rustles, stone knocks, wood creaks, and sand shifts under you.

And so does everyone else's. Every player and animal you can see is walked through the same counter, so a village is full of the sound of villagers moving about, and someone running up behind you is something you can hear.

Landing hurts audibly: a drop plays the real fall sound, quiet under four blocks and heavy over them, plus the block you landed on. Breaking the surface of water splashes, in both directions, and swimming makes strokes.
Sprinting kicks up the ground behind you, in the colour of what you are running across — green off grass, pale yellow off sand, white off snow — and a hard landing throws up a bigger cloud of it.

Your own attacks sound like attacks. The five sounds vanilla picks between — weak, strong, knockback while sprinting, and the crit — are chosen the same way it chooses them, from how far your cooldown had recharged and whether you were falling. A critical hit throws its sparks over whoever you hit.

A totem of undying spends itself in front of you. When one saves anybody in sight, the totem is thrown up across the middle of the screen, growing and fading over two seconds, with its golden particles and its sound.

Twenty-six of the small moments the game keeps to itself now happen. Taming smoke when a wolf refuses you and hearts when it accepts; hearts over two animals in love; a villager's angry cloud, its pleased sparkle, its sweat; a wolf shaking the water out of its coat; a sheep pulling up a mouthful of grass; an iron golem's poppy; a witch's brew; a shield taking a hit and a shield breaking; thorns; drowning; burning; a piece of equipment giving out; an enderman's teleport; honey sliding; a sniffer's nose in the dirt; a dolphin's delight; a ravager stunned; a zombie villager finishing its cure.
Arrows stay where they hit. A body walking around with arrows in it shows them, one shaft per hit, and bee stingers the same way.
The server can stop a sound it started — a music disc turned off mid-song is now actually silent — and it can turn your head to face something, the way `/teleport … facing` does.
Hovering a linked entity in chat shows its name.

The changelog has pictures. Every release from now on carries screenshots straight out of the client's own renderer — click one and it opens full screen, arrow keys to step through. This release comes with two, and 0.59.0 has been given three.

There is an admin portal at /admin now, and it is sealed behind Cloudflare Zero Trust. Identity is checked twice: once at Cloudflare's edge, before the request ever reaches the server, and again here, where the signed token is verified against Cloudflare's own keys — issuer, audience, expiry and address — by a service that answers 503 rather than ever guessing yes. Fifteen security tests throw forged, expired, wrongly-signed and tampered tokens at it; every one has to bounce.

The portal shows what is actually happening: downloads and update checks per day, visitors and page views, where they came from and what they browse with, the current release with its checksums, disk, certificate expiry, uptime, and the release history. Every number is measured on this server from its own logs — nothing is estimated, and there is no third-party tracker anywhere near it.

Downloads are counted from today. The download folder used to be excluded from logging entirely, so nobody could tell how many people had actually downloaded anything; it now writes its own log, and the portal counts it.
Fixed: /favicon.ico answered 404 two hundred times a month. It answers with the real icon now.

Under the hood: the nginx configuration of the site lives in the repository, a script installs it, and the whole gate can be set up with one command. The client gained a step-and-splash counter, an entity-status table and a title card, all with their own tests — 272 in all, ten more than before.

shots.alt: A server's title, subtitle and action bar — live from a real 26.1 server
The same three lines, with a totem of undying going off across the screen

date: Live entity panels, sitting pets, rowing oars & real weather
items: You can see yourself. Your inventory shows your own player model in its panel, in three dimensions, turning to follow the cursor and leaning with it — wearing the armour you are wearing, holding what is in your hands, cape and all. It is the same renderer that draws the world, drawing you into a picture of your own.
Your mount's screen shows the animal. The black panel a horse, donkey or llama screen used to have is the horse, at vanilla's own size and angle, saddle and barding and all.

Dogs sit. A tamed wolf, cat, fox or panda told to sit puts its hindquarters on the ground, folds its back legs forward under it and braces its front ones — the real game's angles, limb by limb, because a pose in Minecraft is every part being placed by hand.
Cats lie down, a sleeping fox curls up beside them, and a fox on the prowl slinks lower.
Horses rear. A horse or a polar bear standing up swings everything above its hind legs over them in one piece, and those hind legs stay planted where they were.
Boats have oars, and they row. Both of them: the boat you are rowing yourself moves its paddles too, which meant keeping the state the server never sends back to you.

Riding something alive shows its health. The hunger bar gives way to the mount's own hearts — ten to a row, as many rows as the animal has health, seven hearts for a donkey and fifteen for a strong horse — and the air bubbles move up out of their way.
Weather is weather. Rain and snow are drawn with Minecraft's own textures instead of grey slivers: real streaks that scroll as they fall, and flakes that drift and sway.
Snow falls where it is cold. Every column asks its own biome what its climate is, so it snows in a taiga, rains in a forest and stays dry in a desert — and nothing falls through a roof any more.
A boss darkens the world. A boss bar that asks for it dims the sky and closes the fog in around you, the way the Wither and the ender dragon do.
A ghast winding up a fireball turns to face you with its red-eyed shooting face.
Parrots ride your shoulders. Both of them, in their real colours.

Fixed: flowers, grass, saplings — every cross-shaped plant — were shredded into stripes when you stood near them, two faces of the same plane fighting over the depth buffer. They are back-face culled now, exactly as the real game does it, and a field of lilacs finally looks like a field of lilacs.
Fixed: the air bubbles no longer sit on top of a mount's second row of hearts.

Under the hood: the renderer can draw entities inside a GUI panel at all now — a new orthographic pass into a texture of its own that the interface blits like any sprite — the models know what each of their parts *is* so a pose can move them one by one, and the client keeps track of max health from the attributes packet, which nothing in the library exposes. Ten new tests, 262 in all, and two new preview shots: your own inventory, and a row of animals told to sit.

shots.alt: Your own player model, in three dimensions, in your inventory
Sitting wolves, cats and foxes, a rearing horse and a boat under oar
Riding a horse: its hearts take the hunger bar's place

date: Elytra flight, horse jumps, mount inventories & sleeping
items: You can fly on an elytra. Jump once in the air while you are falling and the wings open, and from there you fly by looking: level out and gravity almost lets go of you, point the nose down and the fall turns into speed, pull up and that speed turns back into height. It is vanilla's own flight, term for term, so a dive across a valley carries exactly as far as it should. A firework rocket in your hand still does what a firework rocket does — the server pushes you along it.
Gliding stops you sprinting and stops the view bobbing, because your feet are not on anything.
Horses jump. Hold the jump key and the horse winds up — ten ticks to full power, and leaning on the key longer gives you slightly less, exactly as in the real game — then let go and it leaps.

The jump bar shows the wind-up where the experience bar usually is, and takes the level number with it while it is there. Vanilla swaps the whole widget out, in every game mode, because the jump belongs to the horse and not to you.

Your mount's inventory opens with E. A horse gets its saddle and barding slots, a llama gets its carpet, and a donkey, mule or packed llama gets its chest laid out in as many columns as it is actually carrying — three for a donkey, up to five for a llama. Empty slots show the ghost of what belongs in them.

You sit where you actually sit. The camera now takes the vehicle's real seat and turns with it, so a boat's back seat stays at the back however the boat is pointing, and everyone else sees you exactly where you see yourself. In third person you sit rather than stand, and your legs stop walking.
When the server corrects a boat's position, the boat now takes the correction instead of drifting on with its own idea.

You can sleep. Get into bed and the world washes over in vanilla's dark blue across five seconds, with a Leave Bed button — and Escape gets you out of bed instead of opening the pause menu, like the real game.
A spectator passes through the world. No collision, no being shoved back out of a wall you flew into: the game mode finally behaves like the game mode.
F3+B draws every entity's hitbox and the line it is looking along; F3+G draws the borders of the chunk you are standing in, yours in yellow and the eight around it in blue.

Teams colour their members. A player on a red team has a red name over their head, the team's prefix and suffix wrap it, and a team that hides its members' nametags — from everyone, or from everyone but its own side — is finally obeyed.
The player list groups teammates together before it sorts by name, so a server's two sides never interleave.
The debug screen says whether you are gliding, sleeping, and what you are riding.
Fixed: reading who you were riding took the entity lock while it was already held, so the client sometimes did not know what was under it at all.

Under the hood: elytra flight, spectator noclip and the elytra sprint rule are three more patches to the physics we ship ourselves, the mount screen is a container the client keeps on its own (nothing in the library knows what a horse inventory is), and the headless harness now rides a real server's animals and reports it. Ten new tests, 252 in total, and four new preview shots: the horse screen, a llama's full chest, a charged jump and the in-bed fade.

date: Pistons push — plus creative mode: flight, the item menu and pick block
items: Pistons move. A piston pushes its blocks across the gap in front of your eyes instead of teleporting them, because the client now works out for itself what a piston is about to move — the server never says. It sends one word, "fired", and both sides run the same rules from there: the twelve-block limit, obsidian and chests refusing to budge, torches and redstone dust breaking rather than travelling, and slime and honey dragging along everything stuck to their sides.
Sticky pistons pull. The head slides back in and the block comes with it, or stays behind when the pulse was too short — the same distinction vanilla makes.
The piston head grows out of the piston as it extends, arm and all, instead of appearing at the far end a tenth of a second later.
A grass block a piston is carrying is still green while it is in the air, and so are leaves. Every loose block the client draws — the ones on a display entity too — takes its biome colour now.
Note blocks play. The right instrument, at the right pitch for the note it is tuned to, with the coloured note drifting up out of the block.
Creative mode is a mode again. No hearts, no hunger, no armour, no bubbles and no experience bar — the same HUD vanilla leaves you. A spectator gets no hotbar either.
You can fly. Tap jump twice in creative or spectator and you are off the ground: space to climb, sneak to drop, sprint to double your speed, and vanilla's own damping, so it stops where you stop.

The creative menu opens with E. Every item in the game, in the game's own order, nine to a row with a scrollbar and a search box that filters as you type; click one to pick a full stack up and click a hotbar slot to put it there. Right-click takes a single item. Its second tab is your inventory, exactly as before.

Middle-click picks. Look at a block and it comes to your hand — the hotbar slot that already holds it in any mode, a fresh stack in creative. Look at a mob and you get its spawn egg. Torches, redstone, crops, wall signs and lava all hand over the item they are really made of.
The debug screen says which mode you are in, and whether you are flying.

Under the hood: the structure resolver, the stroke it produces and the creative menu's list are all plain functions with tests — twenty-three new ones — and the headless harness now watches a real server's redstone, so a piston firing is checked against the actual game rather than a guess. Two new preview shots: four pistons caught mid-stroke, and the creative menu with a search typed into it.

date: Chests open — plus the beacon, loom, stonecutter and the recipe book
items: Chests open. A chest is not part of the landscape — it is a thing the client draws every frame so that its lid can move — and until now ours could not move at all. Open one and the lid throws itself back and settles shut again half a second later, both halves of a double chest swinging as one, exactly like the game you know. Ender chests, trapped chests and the copper ones all do it too.

Shulker boxes open. The lid lifts half a block and turns three quarters of a turn as it goes, and a box stuck to a wall or a ceiling now stands on the face it was actually stuck to instead of always sitting upright.

Seven chests that were invisible are not any more. Every copper chest past the first stage of weathering — exposed, weathered, oxidized, and all four waxed ones — rendered as nothing at all. They render now. And for the two days a year vanilla wraps the plain chests up for Christmas, so do we.
The enchanting table has its book back. It floats over the table, bobs, and turns to face you when you come close. A lectern with a book on it has one lying open on the stand.

The beacon screen works. All six powers with their real icons, greyed out until your pyramid is tall enough to pay for them, the second power once it is four layers tall, and the tick that applies them.
The loom works. Every pattern you could weave is drawn as the banner it would actually make — your banner, in your dye — in the grid you scroll through, in vanilla's own order.
The stonecutter works. Everything the block in the input slot can be cut into, one button each, filtered out of the full list the server sends when you join.

The recipe book is in. The panel beside a crafting table or a furnace, with the category tabs, a search box that filters as you type, twenty recipes to a page, the ones you can actually make lit up and the ones you cannot greyed out, and the picked recipe laid into the grid as a ghost.
Slimes squash. They flatten as they land and stretch as they hop, which is most of what makes a slime a slime.
More things move on their own: a fish's tail beats side to side, a dolphin's beats up and down, wolves and foxes wag, and the ender dragon's wings finally flap.
A dropped chest or shulker box is drawn as the real thing spinning on the ground, not a flat picture of one.
Typing in the recipe book's search box no longer closes the screen when you type an "e".

Under the hood: a new path for the blocks the client has to draw itself, fed straight out of the mesher, which is what makes the lids possible; the loom's banner pictures are composited once and kept; and five new deterministic preview shots — the containers, the three screens, the recipe book and the animals — so all of it can be checked on any machine, on every build.

date: The world comes alive — ambience, animated mobs, real tooltips & music
items: Blocks make their own ambience now. Almost nothing you see idling in a Minecraft world comes from the server — the client picks a few hundred blocks around you every tick and lets each one decide whether to do something. That whole layer was missing, and the world was technically correct and completely dead. It is there now: torches smoke and flicker, campfires push a slow column with sparks in it, lit furnaces breathe out of their front face, lava pops and steams, nether portals drift purple, end rods throw sparks, cherry leaves shed petals, dripstone drips, crying obsidian weeps, magma bubbles under water, spore blossoms rain green, sculk breathes souls, mycelium puffs spores, brewing stands steam, conduits swirl, enchanting tables pull glyphs off the shelves, powered redstone glows brighter the stronger the signal, and a full beehive drips honey.
Rain lands on things. Where the sky can actually reach the ground, raindrops splash on it.
Eight new particle sprites are in the atlas for all of that — cherry petals, falling leaves, pale-oak leaves, nautilus shells, sculk souls, soul faces, sparks and fireflies.

Mobs move when they are standing still. Parts can now animate on their own clock instead of only riding the walk cycle, which is what made every flying mob look frozen in mid-air. Bees beat their wings fast enough to blur, bats and parrots and phantoms each beat at their own rate, allay and vex wings clap behind their backs, a squid's ring of tentacles ripples instead of hanging like a slab, a ghast's tentacles drift, and the ring of rods around a blaze turns.
Creepers wind up. A lit fuse now swells the creeper and flashes it white, faster and faster, exactly like the second and a half of warning vanilla gives you.

Item tooltips say everything. Hovering a stack now shows what vanilla shows, in vanilla's order: its enchantments by name and level (and no numeral on the ones that only come at level I), the armour trim it carries written out as its pattern and material, a potion's effects with their level and how long they last — harmful ones in red — then the lore, then every attribute modifier with its sign, whether it is unbreakable, whether it is dyed, and how much durability is left.

Drawing a bow looks like drawing a bow. The bow, the crossbow, the shield and the trident each get their own stance instead of all being lifted toward your mouth like food: the bow comes across the view and the string pulls back through its three real sprites, the crossbow cranks level, the shield swings in front of you and turns to face out, the trident winds up over your shoulder.

Music. Vanilla's soundtrack plays again — the menu loops its theme, and in a world a track starts, then the long ten-to-twenty-minute silence before the next, with the Nether, the End and being underwater each scored their own way.

Caves sound like caves. The client keeps vanilla's "mood": it creeps up while the blocks around you are pitch dark and the sky cannot see them, and when it fills you get one of those cave noises from somewhere nearby. It is the reason caves are frightening, and it was missing.

Signs open their editor. Placing a sign now brings up the edit screen with its four lines, a caret you can type into, Enter and the arrows to move between lines, and what you typed goes back to the server.
The HUD stays out of the way. The hotbar, hearts and crosshair no longer draw on top of the screens that cover them.

Under the hood: a new ambience module that is a pure function of a block's name, its state and its neighbours, so every rule is unit-tested without a world; a per-part idle-motion channel in the model format; the bow and crossbow draw sprites baked into the item atlas (they are not registry items, so they were never there); and five new deterministic preview shots — the ambience row, the animated mobs, the full tooltip, the four use stances and the sign editor — so all of it can be checked on any machine, on every build.

date: Maps, advancements, toasts & living screens
items: Maps work. A filled map is no longer a blank sheet: the client now keeps every map the server sends, turns its colour indices into Minecraft's real map palette — grass green, water blue, oak brown, each in the four shades that make a hillside readable — and draws the result wherever a map shows up.
Holding a map opens it. Take one out and you hold it up in both hands, the way the real game does, and read it while you walk.
Maps in item frames. A map in a frame fills the frame, turned in quarter turns like vanilla, so map walls finally show the map instead of a tiny paper icon.

Map markers. Your white arrow points where you are looking, other players show up, banners you named appear in their dye colour, and woodland mansions, ocean monuments, villages and trial chambers get their own icons — all drawn and rotated exactly where the server puts them.

Advancements are real. The server's whole advancement tree now arrives and is drawn in vanilla's window: one tab per branch with its own tiled background, the black-and-white lines from each parent to its children, square frames for tasks, round for goals and spiky for challenges, bright once you have earned them. Drag to look around the tree, hover for the description and how many criteria are still missing.

Toasts. The sliding cards in the top-right corner are here: an advancement completed (green, or purple for a challenge), a goal reached, new recipes unlocked. They slide in, sit for five seconds, slide out, and stack when several land at once.

Statistics are the server's, not a guess. Opening the Statistics screen now asks the server for your real numbers and shows them across General, Items and Mobs — with vanilla's own formatting, so distances read in metres and kilometres, times in hours and days, and damage in hearts.
Furnaces burn. The flame under the fuel slot burns down as the coal is used and the arrow fills as the item cooks — in furnaces, smokers and blast furnaces alike.
Brewing stands bubble. The fuel bar fills with blaze powder, the arrow runs down as the brew progresses, and the bubbles rise in their seven-step loop.

The enchanting table offers. All three offers show: the level numeral, the cost in green, and the unreadable galactic runes vanilla writes them in — drawn with the game's own Standard Galactic Alphabet sheet. Hover to see which enchantment it really is, click to take it.
The anvil names things. The name field takes typing, with a blinking caret, and sends the rename to the server; the level cost shows underneath in green, or "Too Expensive!" in red past 40.
The cartography table shows the map you are working on.

The world border. It has its wall again: the scrolling forcefield tiles standing on the border line, blue while it sits still, green while it grows, red while it closes in — and it follows the server as the border moves.
You can see other people mining. When another player breaks a block, the cracks spread across it in the same ten stages your own mining uses, and vanish the moment they stop.

Explosions. TNT, a creeper, a bed in the wrong dimension: the blast now makes its fireball, its smoke and its sound. The server sends none of that — it is the client's job, and until now nothing happened at all.
Picking things up looks like picking things up. An item flies into whoever collected it over three ticks, with the pickup blip, instead of blinking out of existence.
"You Died!" Dying now opens the real death screen: the red wash, the server's death message, your score, and Respawn / Title Screen — instead of leaving you standing dead in the world.
Written books open. Right-click a signed book and it opens in the vanilla page, with the author's real text wrapped in the same column, the page counter, and the page arrows.

Armour trims render. A trimmed piece shows its pattern in the trim material's own colours — sentry in gold, wild in amethyst, any of the eighteen patterns in any of the materials — built the way the game builds them, by swapping the pattern's palette for the material's.
Nether portals swirl. Standing in a portal fills the view with the portal texture, and nausea draws the sheet vanilla has drawn since it dropped the old warp shader.
Every last German string in the client is gone — the connection and DNS errors, the server-list messages and the address fields are all English now.

Under the hood: eleven more server packets are handled (map data, container properties, advancements, statistics, block destruction, explosions, item pickups, death, book open, the six world-border packets and spectator camera), the HUD is properly hidden behind any full screen instead of drawn on top of it, and five new deterministic preview shots render maps, trims, the border and the cracks, the toasts, the advancement tree, the death screen, the book and three live container screens with no server involved — so all of it can be checked on any machine, on every build.

date: Vanilla lighting, real skies, boss bars, capes & elytra
items: The world is lit the way Minecraft lights it. The client now builds the game's own light table every frame instead of approximating brightness in the shader — which means torchlight is warm orange and flickers, sky light keeps its blue as it dims into night, the falloff follows vanilla's real curve (fast near a torch, slow further out), the Brightness slider works as the gamma curve it actually is, and night vision lifts the darkness without washing out what is already bright. Every surface in the game changed colour with this one.

Smooth lighting. Light is now averaged across each block face instead of being flat per face, so a torch-lit room fades in a smooth gradient across the floor and walls instead of stepping block by block — vanilla's Smooth Lighting, and there is a Video setting to turn it off.

Mobs are lit by the world. Players, animals, dropped items, signs, banners, the item in your own hand — everything now takes the light of the block it is standing in, out of the same table the terrain uses. A creeper in an unlit cave is as dark as the cave; previously every entity glowed at full brightness in pitch darkness.

Dimensions are dark in their own way. The Nether and the End no longer sit at a guessed brightness: each dimension's own ambient light floor applies, so a Nether cave is gloomy rather than pitch black, and the End keeps its pale green cast.
The End has its sky. Standing on the End islands you are surrounded by the real purple starfield box — no sun, no moon, no stars, exactly the sky the dimension has.

Fog takes its colour from the biome. The haze in the distance is now the biome's own fog colour, straight out of the server's registry — which is what makes a crimson forest red, a warped forest teal, a soul sand valley cold and a basalt delta grey, and gives each Overworld biome its own tint through the day.

Going under looks right. Underwater fog now uses the biome's water colour instead of one fixed blue, being frozen in powder snow closes the world down to a few blocks, blindness cuts your view to five, and darkness pulls it in and pulses.

Boss bars. Boss fights have their bar again: the dragon, the wither, raids and every server-made bar, drawn at the top of the screen in all seven colours, with the notched styles segmented the way vanilla segments them, stacked when there is more than one, each with its styled title above it.

Players swim, fly and spin. The elytra flight pose, the swimming and crawling pose, the riptide spin and sleeping are all rendered — a player crawling through a one-block gap lies flat, a player on an elytra flies head-first, a riptide throw spins, and looking up or down tilts the whole body with you.
Capes. A player with a cape wears it: it hangs from the shoulders down the back, lifts as they pick up speed, and leans with them when they sneak.
Elytra wings. An elytra in the chest slot draws its wings — folded against the back on the ground, swept wide open in flight — and hides the cape while they are out, like the real game.

Saddles and animal armour. A saddled pig, strider, horse, donkey, mule, camel or skeleton horse now shows its saddle, horse armour shows in its actual material — leather, iron, gold, diamond, copper, netherite — and an armoured wolf shows its armour.

The F3 screen says something now. The debug overlay gained the biome you are standing in, the dimension, the exact sky and block light at your feet, the in-game day and clock, and a right-hand column showing the block under your crosshair with every one of its state properties — which way a stair faces, whether a door is open, how full a composter is.
Bug fix: torchlight never moved. Vanilla re-rolls a small flicker every tick; block light now does the same, so a torch-lit room breathes instead of sitting perfectly still.

Every last German string in the client is gone: the key-binds screen, the statistics and advancements panels, the connection and DNS error messages, the resource-pack and language notes, and the Discord status are all English now.

Under the hood: the light table lives in one place and is shared by terrain, entities, block entities and the first-person hand, so there is one implementation of brightness rather than three; the mesher carries fractional light levels through the vertex format; and three new deterministic preview shots render a torch-lit room with smooth lighting on and off, every player pose with capes and wings, and the End's sky — with no server involved, so all of it can be checked on any machine, on every build.

date: Block entities come alive — sign text, banners, heads, bells & lightning
items: Signs have words again. Every sign in the world — standing, on a wall, or hanging — now shows its text, drawn with Minecraft's own pixel font at exactly the vanilla size, on both sides, in whatever dye colour the sign was written in. Glowing ink glows: the letters get their bright outline and stay readable in the dark, just like the real game. Shop signs, warp signs, rules boards and spawn instructions are finally readable instead of being blank planks.

Banners fly. A banner shows its base colour and every pattern layer painted onto it — stripes, crosses, borders, the creeper and skull charges, gradients, the lot — stacked in the same order the game paints them, on standing banners and on wall banners alike, with the cloth hanging in front of its pole and swaying gently.

Heads are on the wall. Skeleton, wither skeleton, zombie, creeper, piglin and dragon heads all render as real heads, on the floor at any of their sixteen rotations or mounted on a wall. Player heads wear the actual skin of whoever they belong to, downloaded the same way a player's is — so a wall of trophy heads looks like a wall of trophy heads.

Decorated pots show their pottery. Each of a pot's four faces carries the sherd that was pressed into it, so an archer pot and an angler pot are finally two different objects instead of two invisible ones.
Bells ring visibly: the gold bell hangs inside its frame and swings when someone rings it, damping down over the same two and a half seconds vanilla uses, and it swings towards whoever struck it.

Conduits are alive. The shell renders in the middle of its block, and once its water pocket and prismarine frame are complete — checked exactly the way the game checks it — the cage opens and starts turning.
Campfires cook in the open: the food sitting on a campfire is drawn lying on the fire, one item per corner, so you can see what is on there.
Lightning strikes are visible. A bolt now draws as the real forked, tapering column of light, kinking as it falls and fading out over the half second vanilla gives it.

Mobs look at you. Head rotation is now separate from body rotation, so a villager, a cow or another player can turn their head to follow you while their body stays put — up to the same fifty degrees the game allows before the body swings round too.
Dying mobs fall over. A killed mob plays vanilla's death animation, tipping onto its side over a second before it disappears, instead of blinking out mid-stride.

Riders ride. Anyone in a boat, in a minecart or on a horse now sits on the vehicle with their legs folded, moving with it every frame — previously passengers stood next to their boat and lagged behind it.
Bug fix: wall signs hung a whole block away from the wall they were on. They now sit flush against it, the way the game places them.

Under the hood: the client now reads the block-entity data the server sends with every chunk (sign text, banner patterns, head profiles, pot sherds, campfire contents) and keeps it in step as blocks change and chunks unload; it loads Minecraft's own font definition and glyph pages, with the real per-character widths; and it builds each banner, sign and pot into a single texture once instead of re-drawing layers every frame.

Three new deterministic preview shots render signs, banners, heads, pots, bells, conduits, lightning, the death animation, head turning and a seated rider to images with no server involved, so all of it can be checked on any machine, on every build.

date: Flowing water, animated blocks, shadows, glint & beacon beams
items: Water and lava finally flow. Every fluid surface now has the real vanilla shape: corner-by-corner heights that slope down as the stream thins out, the flowing texture rotated into the direction the water is actually running, proper falling columns that fill their whole block, and the side faces sloped to match — so a waterfall, a river bend and a lava flow all read exactly as they do in the real game instead of as flat blue and orange slabs.

Animated blocks are animated. All 52 animated textures in the game — water, lava, fire, the nether portal, sea lanterns, magma blocks, prismarine, campfires, the seared stonecutter blade and the rest — now play their real frame sequences at the exact vanilla speed, including the smooth cross-fades vanilla uses on lava and portals.
Ocean floors are clean again: kelp, seagrass and every coral now count as water-filled, so a kelp forest is one continuous body of water instead of a blue wall drawn around every single stalk.

Entities cast shadows. Every mob, player, dropped item and vehicle drops the soft round vanilla shadow onto the ground beneath it, projected block by block so it drapes over edges and steps, fades with distance and shrinks away as its owner jumps — the single biggest thing that made entities look like they were hovering.

Enchanted items shimmer. The enchantment glint plays over every enchanted item in your hotbar and in every container, using vanilla's own scrolling, rotating sparkle that follows the item's exact silhouette — enchanted books, tools, weapons and armour are recognisable at a glance again.
Worn tools show their durability. The classic green-to-red durability bar appears under damaged items everywhere item icons are drawn, so you can see at a glance how much life a pickaxe has left.

Beacons shoot their beam. A powered beacon fires the full vanilla beam into the sky — the spinning bright core inside its wide soft glow — and stained glass placed in the beam tints it, layering one colour into the next exactly like the server does.
Falling sand, gravel and anvils are real blocks in flight: a falling block now renders as the actual block that is falling, instead of a nondescript box.
Fishing works visually: the bobber floats on the water at the end of a taut line running back to your rod.
Leashed animals are on a lead — the rope hangs and sags between the animal and whoever (or whatever) is holding it, just like vanilla.
Sheep have wool again. A sheep now wears its fleece as its own layer, and shearing it takes the fleece off — a sheared sheep and a woolly one are finally different animals.
Big piles of dropped items look big: a stack of 64 renders as five overlapping copies, a stack of 20 as three, exactly the way vanilla scales a drop with its size.

End portals and End gateways are no longer invisible holes — both show vanilla's deep starfield surface, so the portal at the bottom of a stronghold and the gateways on the End islands are actually visible.
Going under is a whole different view: submerging closes the world down into a dark blue haze, and swimming in lava blinds you to arm's length — vanilla's underwater and lava fog.

Under the hood: the block atlas can now be updated a sprite at a time while the game runs (that is what makes animated textures possible), textures can be uploaded as tiling sprites, and a new deterministic preview mode renders fluids, animated blocks, shadows, beams, leads and portals to images with no server involved — so every one of these can be checked on any machine, every build.
Bug fix: the potion-effect icons in the headless HUD check were being freed by the UI layer before they could be drawn, and now stay put.

date: Tropical fish, fire, dyed collars & charged creepers
items: Tropical fish finally look like tropical fish — both real body shapes (the small "kob" and the large flat body) render with their true two-tone colouring: a base body colour plus a pattern overlay in a second colour, so every one of the thousands of naturally-spawned varieties shows up as its own distinct fish instead of a plain box.

Any burning entity now has real fire — an animated flame that always faces you and licks up around the mob or player, so you can see at a glance what's standing in lava, caught in sunlight or hit by a flame enchant.
Tamed cats and wolves wear their collars — the collar is drawn over the pet in whichever of the 16 dye colours its owner chose, so your pack is easy to tell apart at a distance.
Charged creepers show their blue electric aura — the crackling energy shell renders over the creeper so a lightning-charged creeper is unmistakable before it gets close.

Under the hood this is the first release to ride the new faster pipeline end to end: because only the client changed, the whole website rebuild is skipped and the new version still appears on the site the moment it ships.

date: Armor stands strike a pose — plus XP orbs, salmon sizes & faster releases
items: Armor stands now strike a pose — they render as the real stand and copy the exact pose the server sets, instead of standing stiff.
Every joint is posed: head tilt, body lean, both arms and both legs each turn to their own angle — so custom-posed stands (statues, sitting figures, pointing signs, decorations) finally look right.
Small armor stands render at half size, and the arms and the stone base plate appear or hide exactly as the server configured them.
Experience orbs render as real glowing orbs — a small green sprite that always faces you and shimmers green↔yellow — instead of blank boxes, so scattered XP is easy to spot.
Salmon now come in their three real sizes — small, medium and large — matching what the server spawned.

Under the hood, releases now ship faster: the changelog is served live alongside the download manifest, so a new version appears on the website the moment it's out without rebuilding the whole site each time.

date: Display entities render — holograms, block & item displays
items: Display entities render — the block, item & text displays servers use for holograms, shops and decorations
Block displays show their real block under the full vanilla transform (translation, scale and both rotations)
Item displays show the item's icon, scaled and rotated exactly as the server placed it
Text displays float as a hologram label, reusing the crafted nametag path
Item-display icons are now double-sided so they never vanish edge-on at any camera angle

date: Minecarts render — the cart plus its cargo (chest, furnace, TNT, hopper & more)
items: Minecarts now render as real minecarts instead of boxes — the open-top cart in its proper shape, and each kind carries its cargo: chest minecarts show a chest, furnace minecarts a furnace, TNT minecarts a block of TNT, plus hopper, spawner and command-block carts.
(Boats and rafts of every wood, including chest boats, already render with their real hull — minecarts complete the set of rideable vehicles.)

date: Projectiles & primed TNT render — arrows, thrown items, fireballs & lit TNT
items: Projectiles and primed TNT now render for real instead of as blank boxes.
Thrown items fly as their true icon: snowballs, eggs, ender pearls, thrown potions, fire charges/fireballs, firework rockets, experience bottles and more.
Arrows and spectral arrows are drawn with their real texture on crossed planes, pointing along their flight path (angled up or down as they arc).
Primed TNT shows the actual TNT block at full size, pulsing white as it's about to blow.
Especially handy in PvP and bedwars, where you can finally see incoming snowballs, eggs, pearls, fireballs and lit TNT.

date: Real particles — every effect drawn as its true sprite, animated & billboarded
items: Particles now look like real Minecraft particles. Instead of little coloured cubes, every effect the server sends is drawn as its true sprite on a camera-facing billboard — flames and soul flames, smoke, crit and enchanted-hit sparks, hearts, notes, splashes and bubbles, explosions, portal shimmer, angry/happy villager puffs, dripping water and more. Animated effects (smoke, explosions, spell swirls) step through their real animation frames over their lifetime, and coloured effects like redstone dust keep their tint.
Under the hood the vanilla particle sprites are packed into one atlas and billboarded with alpha blending, so bursts stay cheap even when there are lots of them.

date: Item frames show their contents — items, rotation, glow frames & empty frames
items: Item frames now show what's inside them. Every frame on the wall renders its held item — as its real flat icon, or as a little 3D block for block items — turned to the frame's rotation, and empty frames show just the wood. Glow item frames get their brighter glowing frame too, and frames hang correctly on walls, floors and ceilings.
This reuses the new flat wall-entity renderer added for paintings, so frames sit flush on whatever surface they're placed on.

date: Paintings render on the wall — all 51 artworks, real size & facing
items: Paintings now hang on the wall for real. Every one of the 51 vanilla artworks renders with its true picture, at its correct size — from the 1×1 Kebab up to the 4×4 Pointer — framed by the wooden edge, and turned to face the right way on whichever wall it's mounted.

Under the hood this adds a proper flat wall-entity render path (front art + wooden back + edges) and reads each painting's art and dimensions straight from the server's painting registry, so modded or datapack paintings show up correctly too.

date: Villagers show their real appearance — biome type, profession & trade badge
items: Villagers now look like real villagers. Each one shows its true appearance, composited from three vanilla layers just like Minecraft does it:
Biome type — the body is hued for the villager's home biome (plains, desert, jungle, savanna, snow, swamp, taiga).
Profession — farmer straw hat, cleric robe, armorer welding mask, librarian, weaponsmith and every other trade wear their real clothing.
Trade level — employed villagers show their stone / iron / gold / emerald / diamond badge on the chest.

Nitwits and unemployed villagers render correctly too (green robe / plain body, no badge). Every reachable type + profession + level combination is pre-composited and cached, so it costs nothing at runtime.

date: More mob variants — cats, wolves & cold/warm animals
items: Cats now show all their breeds — tabby, siamese, calico, ragdoll, persian, british shorthair and more — as sent by the server
Wolves render in all nine coat variants (ashen, woods, snowy, striped, spotted, rusty, chestnut, black and pale)
Cows, pigs, chickens and frogs render their cold, temperate or warm variant
Variants are resolved through the server's data registries, so even custom variants map to the right texture

date: Mob variants — coloured and typed mobs
items: Rabbits, foxes, parrots, llamas, axolotls, horses, mooshrooms and shulkers now show their real colour or type instead of one fixed texture
Parrots come in all five colours and axolotls in all five; horses in every coat colour and llamas in four
Shulkers render in all sixteen dye colours
The per-entity variant is read straight from the server's entity metadata and mapped to the right texture

date: Entity roster complete — bosses, shulker, armor stand & end crystal
items: The Ender Dragon and the Wither now have full 3D models instead of boxes
Shulkers render as their purple shell with the little head peeking out
Armor stands render as a proper wooden stand on a stone base plate
End crystals render as a floating core inside a glass cage on a bedrock base
Every living entity and boss in the game now has a real model — no more placeholder boxes

date: Bestiary expansion — 18 new mob models
items: 18 mobs that used to render as coloured placeholder boxes now have real 3D models
New animal models: axolotl, frog, tadpole, camel, sniffer, armadillo and pufferfish
New illager models: pillager, vindicator, evoker and illusioner, plus the witch and vex
New nether & deep-dark models: strider, hoglin, zoglin, ravager, warden, creaking and the breeze
Allay now has its own winged model; endermite renders as a proper little bug
Bogged skeletons now render with the skeleton model
Nearly every overworld, nether and end mob now renders with a proper model instead of a box

date: Shulker boxes, signs & baby animals
items: Shulker boxes now render in the world (they were invisible block entities) — all 16 colours
Signs render too: standing, wall and hanging signs for every wood type (board + post/bar; text not drawn yet)
Baby animals are drawn at about half size instead of adult-sized

date: 3D mobs, block entities & biome colours
items: 33 real 3D mob models — spider, wolf, fox, villager, enderman, iron golem, snow golem, horse, cat, panda, polar bear, llama, ghast, blaze, dolphin, guardian, cod, salmon, bee, silverfish, parrot, phantom and more — replacing the old coloured-box fallback
Chests, double chests and beds now render in the world (they were invisible block entities with no geometry)
Grass, leaves and water are tinted per biome, read from the server's biome registry, instead of one fixed plains colour

date: Effect/absorption/frozen hearts, pumpkin & spyglass overlays
items: Another big step toward vanilla parity — six new status and screen effects, each drawn exactly like the real game:
Effect-tinted hearts: your health hearts now change color with your effects — green while poisoned, black while withering — just like vanilla.
Absorption hearts: absorption (from golden apples, totems and more) now shows as extra gold "shield" hearts above your health row.
Freezing: standing in powder snow now frosts over the edges of your screen and turns your hearts icy blue once you're fully frozen.
Carved pumpkin: wearing a carved pumpkin on your head now overlays the classic pumpkin blur, so you're peering out through the carved eyes.
Spyglass: using a spyglass now zooms the view in and frames it with the round scope overlay and black bars, exactly like vanilla.
All of these were verified frame-by-frame in a headless render before shipping.

date: First-person item use, lava overlay, blindness & hotbar cooldowns
items: A big step closer to vanilla Minecraft — four new feedback features, all matching how the real game looks and feels:
First-person item use: eating, drinking, drawing a bow or blocking now raises the item toward your face with the vanilla eat/drink shake, instead of just sitting still in your hand.
Lava overlay: sinking into lava now fills the screen with the dense, near-opaque orange wash from vanilla, so you can tell at a glance you're submerged.
Blindness & Darkness: the Blindness and Darkness effects now darken the world the way they do in vanilla — the surroundings fade away while your HUD stays readable, and Darkness pulses in waves.

Hotbar cooldowns: items on a use-cooldown (ender pearls, chorus fruit, shields, and more) now show the shrinking white sweep over their hotbar and off-hand slots, so you can see exactly when they're ready again.

date: Potion effects HUD
items: Active potion effects now show in the top-right of the screen, just like vanilla: each effect's icon in a framed box, its level as a roman numeral, and the remaining time counting down (turning red in the last few seconds).

date: Item name popup & underwater tint
items: The name of the item you just selected now pops up above the hotbar and fades away, exactly like vanilla — a custom name if it has one, otherwise the item's normal name.
Being underwater now tints the whole view blue, like vanilla's water overlay (before, going under water only changed the air bubbles).

date: 3D dropped blocks
items: Dropped blocks on the ground now tumble as their real 3D cube — the block's actual textures, spinning — instead of a flat icon, exactly like vanilla item-drops.
All dropped items now bob gently up and down.

date: Sunset glow & slime models
items: Sunrises and sunsets now glow: a soft warm haze radiates around the sun as it sits near the horizon at dawn and dusk, fading out by full day and hidden during rain — just like vanilla.
Slimes and magma cubes now render as their green cube (scaled to the slime's size) instead of a plain coloured box.

date: 3D blocks in hand & weather
items: Held blocks now render as a real 3D cube in your hand — corner-toward-you, with the block's actual textures — instead of a flat icon. This is the usual view on block-heavy servers like bedwars.

Weather: rain and thunderstorms are now shown, with falling rain streaks around you and the sky and daylight dimmed toward an overcast grey during a storm; the sun, moon and stars hide behind the clouds.

date: First-person hand, sun, moon, stars and clouds
items: First-person hand: your arm and the item or block you are holding now show in the bottom-right corner, with a swing when you attack or mine, a raise when you switch items, and a gentle walk bob — exactly like vanilla.
A living sky: a real sun and moon now cross the sky on the day cycle, stars fade in at night, and the sky colour shifts through sunrise, day, a warm sunset glow, and night.
Clouds: a vanilla-style cloud layer drifts slowly across the sky and dims at night.
Left-handed players now correctly hold the selected item in the shown hand.
